prompt.context: Our client is a family-owned grill manufacturer based in the U.S. The client is the market leader but is considering outsourcing their grill production to increase margins. A large scale outsourcing move would be a first for the industry, and the client wants to know if this is a worthwhile proposition. There are two options being explored: 1) full outsourcing to a plant in China, 2) outsourcing final production in Mexico with parts provided from China.
prompt.question: Which outsourcing option makes the most sense for the client — full outsourcing to China or outsourcing final assembly to Mexico with parts from China — and is the overall outsourcing move worthwhile?

clarifying_info.q: What is the current production setup?
clarifying_info.a: Production is currently done in a single plant in a small U.S. town.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the client sell?
clarifying_info.a: Three lines of grills: basic, medium, and high-end. Each product line is priced competitively for the respective segment.

clarifying_info.q: Has the client outsourced anything before?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The high-end grill production has been outsourced end-to-end for a couple of years with no drop-off in quality or sales.
Sales have been stable across lines for a few years. Sales are seasonal in nature, so timeliness of delivery is important.
Consumers focus on price, quality, and brand name.
The client is the market leader in a fairly concentrated market. No specifics on other companies' shares.

clarifying_info.q: What are the shipping container specs?
clarifying_info.a: Containers can hold 2,000 cubic feet of grills or 5,000 pounds of raw materials. An average grill is 4 cubic feet and 40 lbs.

framework: 1. Cost criteria (apply to each option): Production — input costs (raw materials), manufacturing costs (labor, resources, overhead); Distribution — transportation costs, sales force; Upfront costs — new infrastructure, joint venture/partnership costs
2. Products: Consumer preferences (Made in US?, quality, mix)
3. Company: Experience in outsourcing, domestic PR (layoffs, re-organization), ability to work in new countries with new partners

questions.prompt: Calculate how many grills fit in one shipping container under each option and interpret the cost implication.
questions.guidance: A strong answer recognizes the key asymmetry: finished grills are bulky (volume-constrained) while raw parts are weight-constrained but pack more efficiently. China ships finished grills (volume constraint); Mexico ships raw parts then assembles (weight constraint). The candidate should compute both figures and conclude that China ships 4x more units per container, making distribution costs roughly half those of the Mexico option.

math.setup: Container capacity: 2,000 cu ft OR 5,000 lbs. Average grill: 4 cu ft, 40 lbs.
steps: China option (ship finished grills, volume-constrained): 2,000 cu ft / 4 cu ft per grill = 500 grills per container
Mexico option (ship raw materials by weight, then assemble): 5,000 lbs / 40 lbs per grill-equivalent = 125 grills-worth of materials per container

Ratio: 500 / 125 = 4x more grills shipped per container under China option, meaning distribution cost per grill is ~1/4 as much (i.e., Mexico distribution costs are ~4x higher, or China distribution costs are roughly half of Mexico's on a per-unit basis)
math.answer: China option: 500 grills per container. Mexico option: 125 grills-worth per container. China has ~4x the shipping efficiency; distribution costs under China are roughly half those of Mexico.

questions.prompt: Beyond shipping, what other cost and business factors should be compared between the two options?
questions.guidance: Raw material costs are identical because parts are sourced from China in both cases. Key differentiators are: (1) wage and overhead costs — wages roughly the same between China and Mexico, overhead slightly higher in Mexico; (2) partner/setup costs — client already has a Chinese partner (can expand existing relationship), but would need to find a new partner in Mexico; (3) timeliness risk — seasonal sales make on-time delivery critical; longer or less-established supply chains increase risk.

recommendation: Outsource all production to China (Option 1). Distribution costs are approximately half those of the Mexico option, the client already has an existing Chinese partner with a proven track record (high-end grills outsourced with no drop-off in quality or sales), and there is no expected drop-off in revenue.
risks: PR and company morale impact from job cuts in the small U.S. town where the current plant is located
Scalability of the Chinese production center to handle full volume
Operational difficulty in managing a fully offshore supply chain
next_steps: Evaluate a plan to gradually shift production to China rather than an abrupt cutover
Explore possible company-sponsored initiatives (e.g., re-training programs or plant repurposing) to replace or offset jobs lost in the local town
